key_facts: **DFSP** is a rare, slow-growing, locally aggressive sarcoma of the dermis; metastasis is rare.
Firm, skin-coloured or red-brown **plaque that slowly enlarges** over years, then develops nodules; trunk and proximal limbs.
Often mistaken for a keloid, dermatofibroma or scar: biopsy any enlarging firm plaque.
Treatment: **Mohs** or wide excision; imatinib for unresectable disease; long-term follow-up for recurrence.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: A rare, locally aggressive, low-grade **cutaneous sarcoma**. It infiltrates widely beneath clinically normal skin ("tentacles") and recurs if under-excised. Metastasis is rare (<5%) and mostly follows fibrosarcomatous transformation or repeated recurrence.

sub: Adults 20–50; about 1 per million per year; any ethnicity.

ul: Over 90% carry the translocation **t(17;22)** (often as a ring chromosome), fusing **COL1A1–PDGFB**. This drives autocrine PDGF receptor stimulation and is the rationale for **imatinib** in unresectable or metastatic disease.
Histology: storiform spindle cells infiltrating fat in a "honeycomb" pattern; **CD34 positive, Factor XIIIa negative** (contrast DF).
**"It's just a keloid"**: a keloid follows injury; DFSP enlarges without one.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: A gene fusion makes tumour cells **produce their own growth factor** (PDGF-B).

mech.t: PDGF-B stimulates its own receptor, driving proliferation (imatinib target).
Tentacle-like extensions spread far beyond the visible edge: hence Mohs.
mech.caption: DFSP: slow plaque, then nodules, with deep tentacle-like extension.

histo: Storiform spindle cells infiltrating fat in a honeycomb pattern; CD34+, factor XIIIa–.

ul: Adults aged 20–50; trunk (especially chest and shoulder), proximal limbs, head and neck.

Starts as a slowly enlarging, firm, skin-coloured, pink-violet or brown **indurated plaque**, often mistaken for a scar, keloid, morphoea or DF for years, the same lesion a year apart). Later it becomes **protuberant and multinodular**.

Variants: pigmented (Bednar tumour), atrophic (looks like morphoea), and childhood/congenital forms. The the [skin cancer](condition:basal-cell-carcinoma) notes the course summary notes DFSP can **mimic a keloidal BCC**.
Deep incisional or punch biopsy that includes subcutis (shave biopsies miss it). CD34 immunohistochemistry; FISH/RT-PCR for COL1A1–PDGFB when needed.
MRI for large or recurrent tumours to define deep extent. Chest imaging only for fibrosarcomatous or metastatic disease (specialist).
MRI for large / recurrent tumours; chest imaging only if fibrosarcomatous / metastatic.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses

ddx.name: Keloid / hypertrophic scar
ddx.f: Injury history: beware a ‘keloid’ without one.

blocks: DF (smaller, dimple sign), keloid/hypertrophic scar (history of injury, but beware a "keloid" that appeared without one), morphoea, lipoma, epidermoid cyst, metastasis, other sarcomas, and in children vascular malformation.

ul: **IP role: suspicion and referral only.** Any "scar", "keloid" or "DF" that keeps enlarging, is >2–3 cm, or is nodular on the trunk goes to dermatology urgently (the local skin cancer or sarcoma pathway). NG12's sarcoma recommendation is a reasonable primary-care route where dermatology access is slow.

Specialist treatment: **surgery with complete peripheral and deep margin assessment** (Mohs or "slow Mohs"/staged excision with en-face margins) gives lower recurrence rates than conventional wide local excision with 2–3 cm margins, and spares tissue. European consensus (EORTC/EADO 2015, updated 2022) prefers margin-controlled surgery. Radiotherapy is for positive margins that cannot be re-excised. **Imatinib** is for unresectable or metastatic PDGFB-rearranged disease.
Follow-up: clinical, with recurrence most likely within 3–5 years.

ladder.t: Enlarging ‘scar’, ‘keloid’ or ‘DF’, > 2–3 cm, or nodular on the trunk → **urgent** dermatology (skin cancer or sarcoma pathway; NG12 sarcoma route if access is slow).
**Margin-controlled surgery** (Mohs / slow Mohs) preferred (EORTC / EADO) over WLE with 2–3 cm margins. Radiotherapy for positive margins that can’t be re-excised.
CYP3A4 interactions; warfarin; caution with high-dose paracetamol.

refer.t: A ‘dermatofibroma’ or ‘keloid’ that keeps growing, is > ~3 cm or becomes nodular: exclude **DFSP**.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: A ‘dermatofibroma’ or ‘keloid’ that keeps growing, is larger than about 3 cm or becomes nodular: refer to exclude **DFSP**.
Local recurrence; fibrosarcomatous transformation (higher metastatic risk).

pearls: "A keloid without an injury is not a keloid until proved otherwise."
Imatinib interactions (CYP3A4; warfarin; paracetamol hepatotoxicity at high doses) are worth knowing if a patient on it presents to primary care.
